catalog_quote: [p.78] As a general structural pattern, the reflexes of the inherited Proto Mirndi prefixes can be reconstructed as bearing primary word-level stress in Proto Yirram. (208) *ná-yipi ‘man’s daughter’: Jam/Ngali ná-yipi, Nung nya-ná-yipi ... *ná-wurla ‘female subsection term’: Jam ná-wurla, Nung nya-ná-wurla *ná-wuya ‘nose of a female’: Nung ni-ná-wuya *jú-wuya ‘nose of a male’: Jam/Ngali jú-wiya, ni-y-úya ‘nose of a male’ In productive prefixation systems in Australian languages, primary stress is preferentially on the root. Consequently, in words consisting of a monosyllabic prefix + polysyllabic root, the stress is on the first syllable of the root. The appearance of stress on the prefix in such word forms is an indicator of lexicalisation. [p.28] The acute accent indicates primary stress. [p.29] In its non-reduplicated form, this verb is one of those verbs in the Yirram languages where synchronically the root does not attract stress. (74) ‘1SG-come-PP’ ngá-ruma-ny *nga-rúma-ny There are two factors which favour this pattern. The initial syllable of the root is light and its onset is an approximant.

(208) *ná-yipi 'man's daughter': Jam/Ngali ná-yipi, Nung nya-ná-yipi.. *ná-wuya 'nose of a female': Nung ni-ná-wuya.. Consequently, in words consisting of a monosyllabic prefix + polysyllabic root, the stress is on the first syllable of the root. The appearance of stress on the prefix in such word forms is an indicator of lexicalisatio…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root (stem); productive noun-class and pronominal prefixes are unstressed (Nung nya-ná-yipi, ti-y-ámirra, nya-n-ámirra). Where a historically prefixed word has been lexicalised, the old prefix is now the first stem syllable and carries the stress (ná-yipi; tí-y-imij, nyá-na-mij with short roots). For unprefixed words this amounts to initial stress, matching the sister varieties Jaminjung/Ngaliwurru (Schultze-Berndt 2000:42: stress on the first syllable of the phonological word).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Nungali. For Jaminjung/Ngaliwurru, Schultze-Berndt 2000:42 says the inflected verb receives secondary stress after a main-stressed coverb.
new_statements.exceptions: Harvey 2008:29 (ex. 74): in the Yirram languages the 'come' verb root synchronically fails to attract stress (Jam ngá-ruma-ny, stress on the pronominal prefix) because 'the initial syllable of the root is light and its onset is an approximant'. Schultze-Berndt 2000:42 (Jaminjung/Ngaliwurru only): in words longer than two syllables, heavy non-initial syllables may attract stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Comparative-historical monograph, not a synchronic phonology: the stress marks are on citation-form Nungali words (kin terms, subsection terms, verb paradigms) drawn from Harvey's own 1996 Nungali fieldwork and Harvey & Schultze-Berndt (MS); the rule sentence is stated as a generalisation about Australian prefixing systems / Proto Yirram and applied to the Nungali data, not as a Nungali-specific stress rule. Word level, morphological words with prefixes.
new_statements.identity_note: Harvey 2008:3 treats Nungali as a distinct language but notes it may instead be 'a highly divergent Jaminjungan dialect' (Harvey & Schultze-Berndt MS); the stress-marked forms are Nungali proper (nung1291). The explicit stress rule quoted from Schultze-Berndt 2000:42 is for Jaminjung/Ngaliwurru (djam1255; dialects jami1236, ngal1294), from which Nungali data were excluded. AIATSIS code is N28 per Wikipedia (the N27 URL tried first was unverified).

sources.locator: p. 78, §7.4 (example 208 and following paragraph); PDF page 88 of the ANU Open Research file. Supporting: p. 29 §5.2 ex. 74 (root failing to attract stress); pp. 83-84 tables 214-216 with stress-marked Nungali subsection terms.
sources.note: No synchronic phonology of stress (§3.1 is segmental only). Acute accent marks primary stress on Nungali citation forms (p.29 ex.74; p.78 ex.208; pp.83-84 subsection terms ti-y-úrla, tí-y-imij, ti-y-ámirra, nya-n-ámirra). p.78: in productive prefixation systems primary stress is on the root, i.e. first syllable of the root after a monosyllabic prefix; stress on a prefix indicates lexicalisation (Nung nya-ná-yipi). p.29: in Yirram, roots whose first syllable is light with an approximant onset fail to attract stress (Jam ngá-ruma-ny).

sources.citation: Schultze-Berndt, Eva. 2000. Simple and complex verbs in Jaminjung: A study of event categorisation in an Australian language. PhD, KU Nijmegen (MPI Series in Psycholinguistics 14). pure.mpg.de item_2057716 / hdl 2066/147040
sources.note: §2.1.4 Stress, p.42 (Jaminjung/Ngaliwurru only; Nungali data explicitly excluded, p.8): 'Primary word stress generally falls on the first syllable of a phonological word. However, in forms longer than two syllables, heavy syllables may attract stress when they are in non-initial position.' In complex verbs main stress on the coverb, verb gets secondary stress. p.15 lists the Nungali sources: Capell 1938 notes, Bolt 1967 fieldnotes compiled as Bolt et al. 1971b, Harvey 1996 fieldwork, Hoddinott & Kofod 1976a-c.
